summary:
Antariksha is an AI health guardian for astronauts on deep-space missions. On Mars, a message to a doctor on Earth can take up to 24 minutes, which is far too slow in a medical emergency. Antariksha puts the intelligence on board.

We developed a web platform with three role-based views: the astronaut, the base-station doctor and the mission commander. Because no real suit was available, we built a scenario console that simulates suit-sensor data: eight vital signs, including heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure, body and skin temperature, breathing rate and sweat level.

Our Vitals Condition Model is a multinomial logistic regression we designed and trained ourselves. It compares every reading with normal ranges adjusted for spaceflight, using published research, and with each astronaut’s personal baseline. It then classifies nine conditions and reaches 99.9% accuracy on held-out test cases. It explains every alert, suggests a remedy and medicine from the onboard kit, catches early warnings before readings leave the normal range, and avoids false alarms during exercise.

Within seconds, the astronaut and commander get an alert with a siren, and the doctor receives the full case and can add treatment. Antariksha gives crews care that doesn’t wait for Earth.
details:
Antariksha is an AI health monitor for astronauts on deep-space missions, where a message to Earth can take up to 24 minutes. Because no real suit was available, our scenario console simulates suit data: 8 vital signs, including heart rate, oxygen, blood pressure, temperature, breathing rate and sweat level. Our own trained model, a multinomial logistic regression, runs on board. It compares each reading with spaceflight-adjusted normal ranges and with the astronaut’s personal baseline, detects 9 conditions with 99.9% accuracy on unseen test cases, and explains why. Within seconds, the astronaut and commander get an alert with a siren, along with first-aid steps, a remedy and medicine from the onboard kit, and the doctor receives the full case and can add treatment. It catches early warnings before readings leave the normal range and avoids false alarms during exercise.

We built it with TypeScript, Next.js (React), Tailwind CSS, an Upstash Redis shared store and Vercel hosting, plus Vitest and Playwright for testing. A second model was trained on the public PhysioNet dataset. We focused on crew autonomy under communication delay, safety (the doctor stays in charge, with no doses shown), explainability, privacy by role, and honesty about our simulated data. The result is care that doesn’t wait for Earth.
